title: Does every finite-template decision promise CSP have a P/NP-hard dichotomy?
formal: For every pair of fixed finite relational structures A,B of the same finite signature, with a homomorphism A→B, is the decision promise problem of distinguishing I→A from I↛B either solvable in deterministic polynomial time or NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one promise reductions?
definitions: A finite relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols R with fixed positive arities a_R. A structure A consists of a finite nonempty domain and, for each R, a relation R^A⊆A^{a_R}. A homomorphism h:I→A is a map on domains such that (v₁,…,v_a)∈R^I implies (h(v₁),…,h(v_a))∈R^A for every R and tuple. The templates A,B and their relations are fixed for each computational problem. Only I varies; its domain and relation tuples are explicitly listed in binary, of total length L. The algorithm must accept all I admitting a homomorphism to A and reject all I admitting no homomorphism to B. On I→B but I↛A, either answer is allowed. A→B makes the yes and no sets disjoint. Polynomial time means one deterministic algorithm for the fixed pair, halting on every input in O(L^c), with c and hidden constants allowed to depend on A,B. NP-hardness means a deterministic polynomial-time map from 3-SAT formulas φ to structures I_φ such that satisfiable φ yield I_φ→A and unsatisfiable φ yield I_φ↛B. The question is about deciding the promise, not producing a B-valued assignment. No uniform algorithm for classifying templates is required.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated disjunction for every fixed finite pair, or exhibit a finite pair whose promise problem is neither polynomial-time solvable nor NP-hard under the specified reductions. The two alternatives are exclusive only under P≠NP. An algorithmic criterion covering just one relaxation, a dichotomy for a subclass, or a classification conditional on an additional hardness conjecture does not settle the universal unconditional statement.
context:
Ordinary constraint satisfaction asks whether a collection of local requirements can all hold simultaneously. Promise CSPs keep two versions of each requirement: the input is guaranteed to admit a solution satisfying the stronger version, while the relaxed task uses the weaker one. For graph colouring, A=Kₖ and B=K_c with k≤c produces the decision task of distinguishing k-colourable graphs from graphs that are not c-colourable. Graphs in between impose no decision requirement.

When A=B, the promise disappears. Bulatov and Zhuk independently proved in 2017 that every finite-template CSP is either in P or NP-complete. The present question asks whether a comparable exclusion of intermediate complexity survives arbitrary finite promises. It does not follow merely by applying the classical theorem to A and B separately: the relaxed task can be easier than either endpoint CSP.

A concrete tractable example promises that each listed triple of Boolean variables can have exactly one 1 and asks only for a not-all-equal assignment. Solve the equations x+y+z=1 over the integers, then map positive values to 1 and nonpositive values to 0. No such triple can become all zero or all one. Barto proves that this tractability cannot be explained by sandwiching the pair through a tractable finite-domain CSP, unless P=NP. Finite templates can therefore need an infinite intermediate domain in this natural algorithmic framework.

The algebraic approach studies operations that combine several A-solutions coordinatewise into one B-solution. These polymorphisms capture useful structure for algorithms and reductions, but their input and output domains can differ, preventing the direct use of all the composition arguments available in ordinary CSP. The survey emphasizes that a full dichotomy was not yet backed by enough evidence to be asserted as a settled consensus conjecture; this card poses it as a precise open question.

Important subclasses are classified. Brakensiek and Guruswami obtain a dichotomy for symmetric Boolean promise CSPs allowing negations, with tractable cases going beyond a direct reuse of Schaefer’s classical Boolean CSP classification. That theorem does not classify all Boolean templates or all finite domains.

The 2026 work of Banakh, Barsukov, and Nakajima expands the logical viewpoint by relating Promise MMSNP to finite-domain PCSPs. It also classifies a family defined by forbidden monochromatic cliques under the Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture. Both the restricted family and the additional assumption matter: this is not an unconditional classification of every finite template pair.
why: The main classification question for constraint satisfaction with promises, encompassing approximate colouring and many local relaxation tasks. A resolution would determine whether finite constraint languages force a sharp tractability boundary even when their exact and relaxed solutions differ.

importance.reason: A broad structural question extending the finite CSP dichotomy into approximation and promise problems, with connections to algebra, topology, and optimization.

progress.text: Bulatov proves the finite-domain CSP dichotomy, settling the special case A=B.
Zhuk independently proves the finite-domain CSP dichotomy by a different algebraic algorithm.
Brakensiek and Guruswami establish a symmetric Boolean promise-CSP dichotomy with negations and develop the polymorphism framework.
Barto exhibits a polynomial-time finite-domain PCSP that cannot be sandwiched through a tractable finite-domain CSP unless P=NP.
Krokhin and Opršal survey the open classification landscape and explicitly distinguish decision from search PCSPs.
Banakh, Barsukov, and Nakajima prove a Promise MMSNP correspondence and a conditional monochromatic-clique classification at LICS 2026. The full finite-pair dichotomy remains outside the theorem.

status_note: Open classification question in the cited survey, with relevant partial results checked through 10 September 2026. The card asks for an unconditional decision dichotomy over all fixed finite template pairs; it does not assume decision/search equivalence or a complete algebraic classification.
